items.q: The goal of clustering is to:
options: Maximize intra-cluster distance, minimize inter-cluster distance
Minimize intra-cluster distance, maximize inter-cluster distance
items.explain: Good clusters are tight (intra-cluster distance minimized) and well-separated (inter-cluster distance maximized).

items.q: Clustering is a form of:
items.explain: Clustering finds structure in unlabelled data — unsupervised learning.

items.q: A key advantage of hierarchical clustering over K-means is that it:
options: Does not require specifying the number of clusters in advance (cut the dendrogram)
items.explain: Hierarchical clustering outputs a dendrogram; you cut it at any level to get any number of clusters — no need to pre-set k.

items.q: In single-link (MIN) agglomerative clustering, the distance between two clusters is the:
options: distance of the closest pair of points
distance of the farthest pair of points
items.explain: Single link = MIN = the closest pair. (Complete link = MAX = farthest pair; group average = mean of all pairs.)

items.q: For clusters C1={a,b}, C2={c,d,e} with pairwise distances {3,4,5,2,3,4}, the complete-link distance is:
items.explain: Complete link = max{3,4,5,2,3,4} = 5. (Single link would be min = 2.)

items.q: Agglomerative clustering is ___ while divisive clustering is ___.
items.explain: Agglomerative = bottom-up (merge from singletons); divisive = top-down (split from one big cluster).

items.q: The two alternating steps of K-means are:
options: Assignment (to nearest centroid) and Update (recompute centroids as means)
items.explain: Assign each point to its nearest centroid, then recompute each centroid as the mean of its points; repeat to convergence.

items.q: The time complexity of K-means is:
items.explain: $O(n K I d)$ — n points, K clusters, I iterations, d attributes.

items.q: Why do K-means results vary from run to run?
options: Initial centroids are chosen randomly, and it converges to a local optimum
items.explain: Random initial centroids + convergence to a local (not global) optimum → different runs can give different clusterings.

items.q: Why can't you choose K by simply minimizing SSE?
options: SSE always decreases as K increases (reaching 0 at K=n)
SSE only works for text data
items.explain: More clusters always reduce SSE, so minimizing it favours K=n. Use the elbow method instead.

items.q: Bisecting K-means works by repeatedly:
options: splitting the cluster with the largest SSE using K-means (K=2)
items.explain: It starts with one cluster and repeatedly splits the highest-SSE cluster into two (via K-means, K=2) until #clusters = K — less sensitive to initialization.

items.q: For document/text data, the preferred proximity measure in K-means is:
items.explain: Text uses cosine similarity (cohesion = similarity to the cluster centroid); Euclidean is a poor measure for sparse high-dim word vectors.

items.q: K-means can be viewed as a special case of EM in which:
options: assignments are hard (each point to one cluster) with equal spherical covariances
items.explain: K-means = hard-assignment EM for a Gaussian mixture with equal spherical covariances and equal weights; assignment≈E-step, update≈M-step.

items.q: The first principal component is the direction that:
options: maximizes the variance of the projected data
items.explain: PC1 is the direction of maximum variance; PC2 maximizes variance among directions orthogonal to PC1, etc.

items.q: In PCA, the eigenvectors and eigenvalues of the covariance matrix represent, respectively:
options: the principal components (directions) and the variance explained (importance)
items.explain: Eigenvectors = principal components (directions); eigenvalues = variance explained (rank components by descending eigenvalue).

items.q: Principal components are always:
items.explain: PCA uses an orthogonal transformation → the components are mutually orthogonal and uncorrelated.

items.q: The Singular Value Decomposition factorizes a matrix A as:
items.explain: $A = U\Sigma V^T$ — U (left singular vectors), Σ (singular values), Vᵀ (right singular vectors). Works for non-square matrices.

items.q: In SVD, the singular values are obtained from the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ as:
items.explain: $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$ where $\lambda_i$ are eigenvalues of $A^TA$; the eigenvectors of $A^TA$ are the right singular vectors V.

items.q: The main distinction of deep learning vs classical ML is that DL:
options: automatically learns a hierarchy of features (no manual feature engineering)
items.explain: DL learns features automatically across many layers (a hierarchy of concepts), removing the need for hand-crafted features.

items.q: Why is convolution preferred over fully-connected layers for images?
options: It is sparse (local patches) with weight sharing → far fewer parameters
items.explain: A dense layer on a 224×224×3 image needs >1M weights; convolution connects only local patches and shares filter weights → sparse and efficient.

items.q: For an n×n input, f×f filter, padding p, stride s, the output spatial size is:
items.explain: $O = \frac{n - f + 2p}{s} + 1$. Without padding the image shrinks each convolution.

items.q: The number of parameters in a conv layer with k filters of size f×f over a c-channel input is:
items.explain: Each filter is f·f·c weights; with k filters → f·f·c·k (plus k biases).

items.q: Max pooling:
options: takes the maximum value of each region to down-sample (no learnable parameters)
is a type of activation function
items.explain: Pooling down-samples feature maps by taking a representative value (max or average) per region; it has no learnable parameters.

items.q: AlexNet input is 227×227×3; Conv1 uses 11×11 filters, stride 4, 96 filters. The output is:
A Markov state is one where:
options: the future depends on the entire history
the future is independent of the past given the present (sufficient statistic)
items.explain: A Markov (information) state captures all useful history — the future depends only on the present state.

items.q: A fully-observable RL environment is formalized as a/an:
items.explain: Full observability (O_t = S_t) → a Markov Decision Process ⟨S, A, P, R, γ⟩. Partial observability → POMDP.

items.q: The discount factor γ in the return $G_t = \sum \gamma^k R_{t+k+1}$ controls:
options: how much future rewards are weighted (γ→0 myopic, γ→1 far-sighted)
items.explain: γ ∈ [0,1] weights future rewards: small γ = myopic; large γ = far-sighted. It also keeps the infinite sum finite.

items.q: The Q-learning update rule is $Q(s,a) \leftarrow Q(s,a) + \alpha[\,?\,]$. The bracket is:
items.explain: The bracket is the TD error: target $r+\gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$ minus current estimate $Q(s,a)$.

items.q: The exploration–exploitation trade-off means:
options: balance trying new actions (explore) against using best-known actions (exploit)
items.explain: Exploitation maximizes immediate reward (best-known action); exploration gathers info (new actions). RL must balance the two.

items.q: The scaled dot-product self-attention is computed as:
items.explain: $\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})V$ — scores from Q·Kᵀ, scaled by √dₖ, softmaxed, then weighting V.

items.q: Why do Transformers need positional encoding?
options: Because they process tokens in parallel and otherwise have no sense of word order
items.explain: Unlike RNNs, Transformers process all tokens in parallel, so order info must be injected via positional encodings added to the embeddings.

items.q: Masked (look-ahead) attention in the decoder exists to:
options: prevent each position from attending to future tokens (autoregressive generation)
items.explain: The decoder generates one token at a time; a look-ahead mask adds −∞ to future positions so each word attends only to itself and earlier words.

items.q: Which advance distinguishes GPT-3.5 (ChatGPT) from GPT-3?
items.explain: GPT-3.5 added instruction-tuning and RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) → aligned conversational ability.

items.q: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves an LLM by:
options: retrieving relevant external documents and adding them to the input before generation
items.explain: RAG retrieves relevant docs from a knowledge source and conditions generation on them — overcoming the knowledge cutoff and improving factual accuracy, without changing weights.

items.q: Which technique actually updates the model's weights?
items.explain: Fine-tuning trains the model further on a curated dataset (updating weights). Prompting and RAG change only the input, not the weights.
